newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST - Flatter U.S. yield curve seen into 1998.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Flatter U.S. yield curve seen into 1998.

text.p: The U.S. Tresury yield curve will probably flatten over the next few quarters if bond market players continue to anticipate the Federal Reserve will tighten credit again in 1997, economists said.

Economists polled by Reuters predicted, on average, that short-term yields would rise with an expected increase in the federal funds target rate. Meanwhile, they said yields on the long end should decline in tandem with inflation fears as U.S. economic growth softened.
On average, the 30 experts surveyed on Friday and on Monday forecast the two-year note yield would rise to as high as 6.51 percent by December 1997 and fall back to 6.33 percent by June 1998.
The experts forecast the bellwether 30-year T-bond yield would show a more modest increase to 7.00 percent by December before dipping to 6.78 percent a year from now.

That would assume a spread of about 50 basis points between the two issues by year end, dipping to about a 45-basis-point gap in mid-1998. Currrently, the spread between the two- and 30-year issues is around 67 basis points.
"The Fed is still in a tightening mode," said Bob Barr, deputy chief economist at the U.S. Chamber of Commerce.

"(The yield curve) should get a little tighter on the short end as we expect the Federal Reserve to raise rates one more time," said Barr, who predicted the Fed would boost rates by a quarter of a percentage point at the monetary policy meeting in August.

The latest Reuters Fed poll found that 20 of 37 economists expect the central bank to increase the federal funds to 5.75 percent from 5.50 percent at the next Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting on July 1-2.
More than three-quarters of those surveyed saw a rate hike by the end of August.
The cumulative affects of higher short-term interest rates is expected to weigh down economic growth late this year and into early 1998, said Paul Kasriel, chief economist at Northern Trust.
Kasriel said higher rates coupled with continued strength in the dollar "would be frosting on the cake for that sort of flattening scenario."
Some analysts said that even if the Fed refrains from lifting interest rates in July, market expectations of an eventual Fed hike would still narrow spreads.
"If the market still gets the sense the Fed is still ahead of the curve, then we'll get more curve flattening," said Richard Koss, international strategist at MFR Inc.
Full results of the survey follow.
